guide.takeaway: In Stage 0 (`Lesson S0.4`), you learned that electrical power in Watts (`W`) is $P_{\text{elec}} = V \cdot I$ (Voltage push $\times$ Current flow). guide.takeaway: By **Hooke's Law**, stretching or compressing a spring by displacement $x$ (in meters `m`) creates a restoring force $F_s = -k \cdot x$ pointing back toward $x = 0$, where $k$ is the **spring constant** (stiffness, in **`N/m`**). Because a mass $m$ has momentum, a spring alone makes the mass coast right past $x = 0$ and oscillate back and forth forever! Adding a shock absorber provides **viscous damping** force $F_d = -b \cdot v$ (where $b$ is the damping coefficient in **`N·s/m`**), which opposes velocity $v$ and drains excess kinetic energy into heat.

guide.takeaway: Inside every motor is a coiled wire electromagnet called an **inductor** (measured in **Henries `H`** or **millihenries `mH`**), which stores energy in a magnetic field and fights any sudden change in **current** ($V_L = L \frac{\Delta I}{\Delta t}$). If a MOSFET suddenly switches OFF a $2.0\text{ A}$ motor current in $2.0\ \mu\text{s}$ with nowhere for that current to go, the collapsing magnetic field generates a massive hundred-volt **inductive kickback** spike that punches straight through the MOSFET! Wiring a **flyback diode** in parallel across the motor coil (pointing from the MOSFET Drain **upward** to $+12\text{ V}$) stays off during normal running, but instantly turns on when the MOSFET opens—giving the coil current a safe loop to recirculate and clamping the Drain voltage to $V_{\text{supply}} + 0.7\text{ V} = 12.7\text{ V}$.

guide.takeaway: **Forward Kinematics (`FK`)** answers the question: "Given the motor's joint angle $\theta_1$, where is the tip of the arm $(x, y)$ in the world coordinate frame?" guide.takeaway: A single slotted optical sensor only tells you speed, not direction. An **incremental quadrature encoder** places two sensors (`Channel A` and `Channel B`) a quarter-slot apart ($90^\circ$ phase shift). When `A` rises before `B`, the shaft is turning forward (`+1`); when `B` rises before `A`, it is turning backward (`-1`). idea.title: Open circuits versus short circuits

resources.title: SparkFun — What is a Circuit? ("Short and Open Circuits")

guide.read: Read exact heading **`Short and Open Circuits`**.
guide.skip: Skip the bottom links.
guide.takeaway: An **open circuit** is a broken loop ($R = \infty, I = 0$). A **short circuit** is an unintended near-zero-resistance bypass path ($R_{\text{wire}} \approx 0.05\ \Omega$) directly across a power supply or across both legs of a component. By Ohm's Law ($I = V / R_{\text{wire}}$), a $5.0\text{ V}$ short attempts to draw $I = 5.0 / 0.05 = 100\text{ A}$, starving the rest of the circuit and overheating wires!

S0.4.title: Diodes, LEDs, Forward Voltage Drop (V_f) and Resistor Power Ratings (P = VI)

idea.title: Diodes, LED polarity, and series current-limiting resistor sizing

guide.takeaway: A **diode** is a one-way electrical check valve: current only flows when the **Anode (`+`, longer leg)** is at a higher voltage than the **Cathode (`-`, shorter leg / flat rim)** by at least its **forward voltage** ($V_f \approx 1.8\text{–}2.0\text{ V}$ for red, $\approx 3.0\text{–}3.3\text{ V}$ for blue/white). Once turned on, an **LED** has almost zero internal resistance of its own—connecting it directly across $5.0\text{ V}$ without a series **current-limiting resistor** destroys it instantly!

idea.title: Electrical power dissipation ($P = V \cdot I = I^2 R$) and resistor power ratings

guide.read: Read exact headings **`What is Electric Power?`**, **`Calculating Power`**, and **`Power Ratings`**.
guide.skip: Skip high-voltage AC transmission line math.
guide.takeaway: **Electrical power** ($P$, measured in **Watts `W`** or **milliwatts `mW`**) is the rate at which electrical energy turns into heat or work: $P = V \cdot I$. Substituting Ohm's Law ($V = I \cdot R$) gives $P = I^2 \cdot R = \frac{V^2}{R}$. Standard breadboard resistors are rated for **$1/4\text{ W}$ ($0.25\text{ W} = 250\text{ mW}$)** maximum heat; engineers always keep continuous resistor dissipation below **$50\%$ of its rating ($\le 125\text{ mW}$)** so it stays cool to the touch.

S0.5.title: Virtual Multimeters (Voltmeter vs. Ammeter) and Current-Limited (CC/CV) Bench Supplies

idea.title: Multimeter probing rules (voltmeter in parallel, ammeter in series, ohmmeter unpowered)

guide.takeaway: A digital multimeter (`DMM`) combines three instruments with completely different internal circuits: 1. **Voltmeter (`V` mode):** Has huge internal resistance ($\approx 10\text{ M}\Omega$). Touch its red and black probes **in parallel (across)** the component while power is ON. 2. **Ammeter (`A` / `mA` mode):** Has near-zero internal resistance ($\approx 0.05\ \Omega$, like a bare wire!). You **must break the loop** and wire the ammeter **in series** so current flows *through* the meter. Touching an ammeter in parallel across `5V` and `GND` creates a dead short circuit and blows the meter's internal fuse! 3. **Ohmmeter (`Ω` / Continuity mode):** Injects its own tiny test current; **always turn circuit power OFF** before measuring resistance or continuity.

idea.title: Bench power supply Constant-Voltage (`CV`) versus Constant-Current (`CC`) current limiting

resources.title: SparkFun — How to Power a Project

guide.read: Read exact headings **`Overview`** and **`Variable DC Benchtop Power Supply`**.
guide.skip: Skip solar/LiPo charging sections (covered in Track 01).
guide.takeaway: Unlike a raw battery that will happily dump $50\text{ A}$ into a wiring mistake and melt your breadboard, an adjustable **bench power supply** lets you set **two** knobs before turning power on: a target voltage $V_{\text{set}}$ (e.g., $5.0\text{ V}$) and a maximum current limit $I_{\text{limit}}$ (e.g., $0.10\text{ A} = 100\text{ mA}$ for a logic breadboard). As long as your circuit draws less than $I_{\text{limit}}$, the supply stays in **Constant-Voltage (`CV`)** mode at $5.0\text{ V}$. The instant a short circuit tries to draw more than $I_{\text{limit}}$, the supply switches to **Constant-Current (`CC`)** mode—clamping current to $I_{\text{limit}}$ and folding output voltage down to $V_{\text{out}} = I_{\text{limit}} \cdot R_{\text{load}}$!

S0.6.title: Capacitors — Charge Storage (tau = R*C) and Power-Rail Decoupling

idea.title: Capacitor charge storage and RC time constant ($\tau = R \cdot C$)

guide.read: Read exact headings **`Introduction`**, **`Symbols and Units`**, **`Capacitor Theory`**, **`Charging and Discharging`**, and **`Capacitor Types`**.
guide.skip: Skip **`Capacitors in Series/Parallel`** and **`Application Examples -> Signal Filtering`**.
guide.takeaway: A **capacitor** acts like a tiny, ultra-fast rechargeable bucket that stores electrical charge on two conductive plates separated by an insulator, measured in **Farads (`F`)**—typically **microfarads (`µF`, $10^{-6}\text{ F}$)** or **nanofarads (`nF`, $10^{-9}\text{ F}$)**. Because moving charge onto the plates takes time, **a capacitor's voltage cannot change instantly**. When charged through a resistor $R$, the **RC time constant** $\tau = R \cdot C$ (in seconds) tells you the exact time needed to cover $63.2\%$ of the remaining voltage step (reaching $\approx 99.3\%$ after $5\tau$).

idea.title: Power-rail decoupling (bypass) capacitors

guide.read: Read exact headings **`Application Examples`**, **`Decoupling (Bypass) Capacitors`**, and **`Power Supply Filtering`**.

guide.takeaway: When a heavy load or digital chip suddenly demands a burst of current, the parasitic resistance of long battery wires causes the $5.0\text{ V}$ supply rail to dip ("brown out"), which can reboot a microcontroller mid-motion. Placing a **$0.1\ \mu\text{F}$ ($100\text{ nF}$) ceramic decoupling capacitor** right next to the chip's `VCC` and `GND` pins (paired with a **$100\ \mu\text{F}$ electrolytic bulk capacitor** where power enters the breadboard) supplies that instant current burst locally and keeps the voltage rail rock-steady.

guide.takeaway: Digital pins (`0`–`13`) only distinguish `LOW` ($0\text{ V}$) from `HIGH` ($5\text{ V}$). S0.9.title: Switching Power Smoothly — PWM Duty Cycle and analogWrite()

idea.title: Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) duty cycle and average voltage ($V_{\text{avg}} = \text{Duty} \times V_{\text{cc}}$)

guide.read: Read exact headings **`What is Pulse-width Modulation?`**, **`Duty Cycle`**, and **`Examples`**.
guide.skip: Skip manual ATmega timer-register bit-banging—use `analogWrite()` in Stage 0.
guide.takeaway: An Arduino Uno has no true analog voltage output (`DAC`); its pins can only switch between $0.0\text{ V}$ (`LOW`) and $5.0\text{ V}$ (`HIGH`). To simulate an intermediate voltage, **Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM)** switches the pin between $0\text{ V}$ and $5\text{ V}$ hundreds of times per second. The **duty cycle** is the fraction (or percentage) of each period $T = 1/f$ that the signal stays `HIGH` ($\text{Duty} = T_{\text{on}} / T$). Because your eyes and mechanical motors average out fast pulses, a $25\%$ duty cycle acts like $0.25 \times 5.0\text{ V} = 1.25\text{ V}$, and a $50\%$ duty cycle acts like $2.50\text{ V}$!
